title: Human clinicians outperform AI stethoscope in diagnosing pet heart problems
excerpt: Fourth-year veterinary students matched—and experienced clinicians outperformed—an AI-enabled digital stethoscope in diagnosing heart murmurs and arrhythmias in cats and dogs, according to a new study from North Carolina State University. The study emphasizes the importance of human expertise when using AI-assisted technology, particularly with instruments designed for "universal" usage. The research is published in the Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association.
content_html:
Fourth-year veterinary students matched—and experienced clinicians outperformed—an AI-enabled digital stethoscope in diagnosing heart murmurs and arrhythmias in cats and dogs, according to a new study from North Carolina State University. The study emphasizes the importance of human expertise when using AI-assisted technology, particularly with instruments designed for "universal" usage. The research is published in the Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association.

"Stethoscopes are universal instruments—they're designed to aid in auscultation, or listening to the heartbeat," says Kursten Pierce, assistant professor of clinical sciences and board-certified cardiologist at NC State's College of Veterinary Medicine. "Veterinarians use the same stethoscope that a human physician uses. These new AI-enabled stethoscopes are being adopted by many veterinarians because they have a lot of very useful technical features, such as recording a heart murmur or an EKG.

"However, the diagnostic AI for these stethoscopes is trained on human data, not dog or cat data, and we were hearing from veterinarians who were second-guessing themselves based on the stethoscope's findings. So, we decided to look at an AI-enabled stethoscope's diagnostic accuracy in dogs and cats."

The research team performed auscultation on 105 companion animals: 54 dogs and 51 cats. Each animal was examined by a board-certified veterinary cardiologist, a cardiology resident and a fourth-year veterinary student. The exams were conducted with an AI-enabled stethoscope, and the findings from the human experts were compared with the stethoscope's findings.

In dogs, the doctor's assessment found that 38 (70%) had a murmur and 24 (44%) had an arrhythmia (abnormal heartbeat). Of the 38 dogs with a murmur, the AI software correctly identified 33 (87%). Fourth-year students matched the stethoscope's performance exactly.

Arrhythmia detection told a very different story: The AI stethoscope never classified a single dog as free of an arrhythmia, and while it correctly flagged all six true cases of atrial fibrillation, it also mistakenly labeled 22 additional dogs as having atrial fibrillation when they did not.

In cats, the doctor's assessment found that 22 (43%) had a murmur and only 1 (2%) had an arrhythmia. The AI stethoscope diagnosed a murmur in only 2 of 51 cats—missing 20 of the true murmurs. Veterinary students performed substantially better in cats, correctly identifying murmurs in nearly two-thirds of affected cats.

"The most clinically concerning result to me was cats," says Jake Johnson, cardiology resident at NC State and the first author of the research. "This device essentially couldn't find a murmur, so a tool vets lean on for reassurance could let real disease go undetected—you wouldn't necessarily think about the fact that the diagnostic algorithms are designed based on humans.

"We saw a similar pattern in dogs with arrhythmias: the stethoscope never once called a dog's rhythm normal, and its atrial fibrillation calls were wrong three out of four times. That said, the ECG tracing it captures is genuinely good quality. This tool works best as an adjunct—a quick ECG or a flag worth a second look—not a stand-alone diagnosis."

The researchers hope their results will encourage veterinarians and veterinary students to become better informed about the limitations of these stethoscopes in veterinary care.

"We want to encourage veterinarians to rely on the expertise they've gained through their training and to understand what this tool can and cannot provide in a veterinary setting, so that we continue to provide the best possible care to people and their companion animals," Pierce says.

Publication details

Jake H. Johnson et al, An artificial intelligence–enabled digital stethoscope demonstrates moderate murmur detection in dogs but not cats and unreliable arrhythmia classification in both species, Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association (2026). DOI: 10.2460/javma.26.05.0353

Cardiac auscultation was performed by a veterinary cardiologist, cardiology resident, and clinical year student on 54 dogs and 51 cats. The device interfaces with a smartphone application to perform cardiac auscultation and generate real-time AI-assisted interpretations of murmur presence and cardiac rhythm at each auscultation site; the device and application are designed for use in humans. 北卡罗来纳州立大学的一项新研究显示，四年级兽医学生在诊断猫和狗的心脏杂音和心律失常方面，与具有人工智能功能的数字听诊器相匹配，并且经验丰富的临床医生表现优于该听诊器。 该研究强调了使用人工智能辅助技术时人类专业知识的重要性，特别是使用专为“通用”用途而设计的仪器。 该研究发表在《美国兽医协会杂志》上。

“听诊器是通用仪器，旨在帮助听诊或听心跳，”北卡罗来纳州立大学兽医学院临床科学助理教授和委员会认证心脏病专家库尔斯滕·皮尔斯 (Kursten Pierce) 说。 “兽医使用的听诊器与人类医生使用的听诊器相同。 这些新型人工智能听诊器正在被许多兽医采用，因为它们具有许多非常有用的技术功能，例如记录心脏杂音或心电图。

“然而，这些听诊器的诊断人工智能是根据人类数据进行训练的，而不是狗或猫的数据，我们听到兽医们根据听诊器的结果对自己进行了事后怀疑。 因此，我们决定研究人工智能听诊器对狗和猫的诊断准确性。”

研究小组对 105 只伴侣动物进行了听诊：54 只狗和 51 只猫。 每只动物都由一名经过委员会认证的兽医心脏病专家、一名心脏病住院医师和一名四年级兽医学生进行了检查。 检查是使用人工智能听诊器进行的，并将人类专家的检查结果与听诊器的检查结果进行比较。

在狗身上，医生的评估发现，38 只（70%）有杂音，24 只（44%）有心律失常（心跳异常）。 在 38 只发出杂音的狗中，人工智能软件正确识别了 33 只（87%）。 四年级学生与听诊器的性能完全匹配。

心律失常检测却讲述了一个截然不同的故事：人工智能听诊器从未将一只狗归类为没有心律失常，虽然它正确标记了所有六例真实的心房颤动病例，但它也错误地将另外 22 只狗标记为患有心房颤动，而实际上它们没有。

在猫中，医生的评估发现 22 只（43%）有杂音，只有 1 只（2%）有心律失常。 AI 听诊器仅诊断出 51 只猫中的 2 只存在杂音，漏掉了 20 只真正的杂音。 兽医学生在猫身上的表现要好得多，能够正确识别近三分之二受影响的猫的杂音。

“对我来说，临床上最令人担忧的结果是猫，”北卡罗来纳州立大学心脏病学住院医师、该研究的第一作者杰克·约翰逊（Jake Johnson）说。 “这种设备基本上无法发现杂音，因此兽医依靠的工具可以让真正的疾病不被发现——你不一定会想到诊断算法是基于人类设计的这一事实。

“我们在患有心律失常的狗身上看到了类似的模式：听诊器从未认为狗的心律正常，并且它的心房颤动呼叫四分之三是错误的。 也就是说，它捕获的心电图追踪质量确实很高。 该工具作为辅助工具效果最好——快速心电图或值得再看的标志——而不是独立的诊断。”

研究人员希望他们的结果能够鼓励兽医和兽医学生更好地了解这些听诊器在兽医护理中的局限性。

“我们希望鼓励兽医依靠他们通过培训获得的专业知识，并了解该工具在兽医环境中可以提供什么和不能提供什么，以便我们继续为人们及其伴侣动物提供最好的护理，”皮尔斯说。

出版详情

杰克·H. Johnson 等人，支持人工智能的数字听诊器对狗（而非猫）进行了中等杂音检测，并且对这两个物种的心律失常分类不可靠，《美国兽医协会杂志》（2026 年）。 DOI：10.2460/javma.26.05.0353
